item.prompt: Which statement best expresses the central idea of the passage?
item.correct_answer: An adult recalls the wonder of first seeing flamingos at age six, a thrill that none of his many later sightings ever matched.
choices: A flamingo spreading its crimson wings looks to a young boy like the most angelic creature he could imagine anywhere.
An adult recalls the wonder of first seeing flamingos at age six, a thrill that none of his many later sightings ever matched.
An adult recalls his first long walk across the plain with his brother, taken before he was able to ride off alone.
A young boy walks with his brothers to a river on the plain and sees many kinds of wild birds, among them some tall flamingos.
An adult recalls seeing flamingos at age six as the greatest experience of his life, one that nothing afterward could equal.

distractors.text: A young boy walks with his brothers to a river on the plain and sees many kinds of wild birds, among them some tall flamingos.
quotes: A six-year-old boy walks two miles with his brothers to a river on the pampas and sees lots of wild birds, like ducks, swans, herons and flamingos.
A boy goes on a long walk with his brother to a river and sees many birds, including three tall white-and-rose birds with crimson wings.
distractors.refutation_sentence: It was not for several years that I had an opportunity of seeing the bird again; later I have seen it scores and hundreds of times, at rest or flying, at all times of the day and in all states of the atmosphere, in all its most beautiful aspects, as when at sunset or in the early morning it stands motionless in the still water with its clear image reflected below; or when seen flying in flocks--seen from some high bank beneath one--moving low over the blue water in a long crimson line or half moon, the birds at equal distances apart, their wing-tips all but touching; but the delight in these spectacles has never equalled in degree that which I experienced on this occasion when I was six years old.
distractors.why_not_single_sentence: The sentence never mentions the walk or the variety of birds; it shows the passage builds to the unmatched first sighting, so ruling this out needs a judgement about the whole passage's point, not a wording match.

item.prompt: Which statement best expresses the central idea of the passage?
item.correct_answer: Nature prepares for each coming season while the current one is still going on, forming buds and new growth months before spring.
choices: Trees shed their old leaves in the fall to make room for new buds, and then nature comes back to life each spring.
Some trees, such as oaks and beeches, hold on to their old leaves, while tidier trees like maples drop theirs neatly.
New buds form on trees in late summer, well before the old leaves are ready to drop from their branches.
Nature prepares for each coming season while the current one is still going on, forming buds and new growth months before spring.
The new growing season actually begins in December, since plants are already preparing for spring by early winter.

distractors.text: Some trees, such as oaks and beeches, hold on to their old leaves, while tidier trees like maples drop theirs neatly.
quotes: Some trees like oaks and beeches hang on to their old dead leaves because they can't let go, while tidy trees like maples drop them neatly.
The passage is mainly about how trees lose their old leaves, and why some trees like maples drop them neatly while oaks and beeches hold on.
distractors.refutation_sentence: Nature looks ahead, and makes ready for the new season in the midst of the old.
distractors.why_not_single_sentence: The sentence says nothing about which trees keep or drop leaves; rejecting the option requires recognising the leaf-shedding discussion as an opening example of the broader claim.

distractors.text: The new growing season actually begins in December, since plants are already preparing for spring by early winter.
quotes: Nature's new season really starts in winter, around December, because plants and trees are already getting ready for spring long before it arrives.
distractors.refutation_sentence: It is in late summer, when the new buds are formed on the trees.
distractors.why_not_single_sentence: The sentence does not contain 'December' or 'begins'; a student matching the option's word 'December' lands on the correspondent's claim, which supports it, and only by resolving 'It' to the real start of the season does this sentence refute it.

distractors.text: Trees shed their old leaves in the fall to make room for new buds, and then nature comes back to life each spring.
quotes: Trees lose their old leaves in fall so new buds can grow, and in spring nature comes back to life after the winter.
distractors.refutation_sentence: The new bud is formed in the axil of the old leaf long before the leaves are ready to fall.
distractors.why_not_single_sentence: The sentence does not say leaves are not shed to make room; it states the bud is already formed beside the old leaf before it falls, and the student must infer that the bud therefore does not wait for the leaf to go.

distractors.text: New buds form on trees in late summer, well before the old leaves are ready to drop from their branches.
quotes: New buds are formed on trees in late summer, long before the old leaves are ready to fall.
distractors.refutation_sentence: The egg, the seed, the bud, are all alike in many ways, and look to the future.
distractors.why_not_single_sentence: The option is a true detail, so no sentence negates its words; this sentence shows the bud is one of several examples (egg, seed, bud) of a general pattern, which the student must weigh to see the detail is not the central idea.

key_support: Nature looks ahead, and makes ready for the new season in the midst of the old.
The present season is always the mother of the next, and the inception takes place long before the sun loses his power.
In all cases, before Nature closes her house in the fall, she makes ready for its spring opening.

item.prompt: Which statement best describes the author's response to his correspondent's suggestion that spring really begins in December?
item.correct_answer: He accepts that growth starts before spring but argues the true start comes even sooner, in late summer when trees form buds.
choices: He agrees that spring really begins in December, and he cites wildflowers and skunk-cabbage that are already growing then.
He agrees that spring starts early, and notes that his correspondent places its true start in late summer, when buds form.
He accepts that growth starts before spring but argues the true start comes even sooner, in late summer when trees form buds.
He disagrees, holding that the new season really starts later, in spring, once the weather warms and the flowers bloom.
He rejects his correspondent's view as completely wrong, since every plant forms its buds in late summer and not in December.

distractors.text: He agrees that spring really begins in December, and he cites wildflowers and skunk-cabbage that are already growing then.
quotes: He agrees with the correspondent that spring starts in December, and adds examples like wildflowers and skunk-cabbage already growing then.
He says spring begins in December because the annual cycle of vegetable life starts then and wild flowers already have new shoots.
distractors.refutation_sentence: But the real start of the next season's vegetable life in this sense is long before December.
distractors.why_not_single_sentence: Matching the option's words (December, wildflowers, skunk-cabbage) leads to sentences that support it; this sentence does not say 'he disagrees' but corrects the date with 'But ... long before', and a second sentence ('It is in late summer...') refutes it with no shared wording.

distractors.text: He disagrees, holding that the new season really starts later, in spring, once the weather warms and the flowers bloom.
quotes: He disagrees, because spring really starts in March when it warms up and flowers bloom, not in cold December.
He disagrees; he thinks the new season actually starts later, after the old leaves are gone and things warm up, not as early as December.
distractors.refutation_sentence: It is in late summer, when the new buds are formed on the trees.
distractors.why_not_single_sentence: The sentence does not mention spring, warmth or blooming; it refutes the option by placing the start earlier, not later, and only once 'It' is resolved to the real start of the season.

distractors.text: He rejects his correspondent's view as completely wrong, since every plant forms its buds in late summer and not in December.
quotes: He says his correspondent is completely wrong, because spring actually starts in late summer when all plants form their buds, not in December.
distractors.refutation_sentence: Our earliest spring flower, the skunk-cabbage, may be found with its round green spear-point an inch or two above the mould in December.
distractors.why_not_single_sentence: The sentence never mentions the correspondent or judges him right or wrong; the student must infer that by confirming growth in December the author accepts the correspondent's observations, so he is not rejecting them wholesale.

distractors.text: He agrees that spring starts early, and notes that his correspondent places its true start in late summer, when buds form.
quotes: He agrees with him that spring starts early, and the correspondent adds that it actually begins in late summer when buds form on the trees.
distractors.refutation_sentence: A correspondent, writing to me from one of the colleges, suggests that our spring really begins in December, because the "annual cycle of vegetable life" seems to start then.
distractors.why_not_single_sentence: The sentence does not mention late summer at all; the student must notice that the correspondent's date is December and therefore that the late-summer claim is the author's own correction.

key_support: But the real start of the next season's vegetable life in this sense is long before December.
It is in late summer, when the new buds are formed on the trees.

tiebreak: Both size-2 wrong clusters (c2, c3) and both size-1 wrong clusters (c4, c5) are all selected, so the tie does not change the set; c2 is listed first among the size-2 pair as the passage-anchored lure (the correspondent's December claim really is in the passage, NAEP guide §3.3/§4 item 11), ahead of the prior-belief lure c3.
